raw_case_text:
A 34-year-old male with no family history of autoimmune diseases or thrombotic events and no chronic degenerative diseases began experiencing his current condition on June 9, 2025, at approximately 8:30 a.m. Upon waking up, presenting with sudden onset paresthesia in the upper and lower extremities of the left side of the body, lasting approximately two hours. The initial symptoms were accompanied by muscle stiffness in the left side of the body, generalized weakness, paresthesia in the left side of the face, and predominantly distal dysesthesia, with preserved consciousness and speech. He therefore went to the emergency department, with initial vital signs of blood pressure 126/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 19 breaths per minute, heart rate 88 beats per minute, saturation 94% in ambient air, and temperature 36.2 degrees.
Neurological evaluation of the left lower extremity revealed hyperreflexia, increased muscle tone, and a positive Babinski sign, consistent with left upper motor neuron (UMN) syndrome. He had a strength of 3/5 on the Daniels scale in his left upper limb and 3/5 in his left lower limb, with decreased fine sensitivity in the ipsilateral upper limb. His initial National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score was 12 points, corresponding to a moderate neurological deficit, and his Glasgow Coma Scale score was 15.
Due to suspicion of a stroke, a plain computed tomography (CT) scan of the skull was performed, which revealed an ischemic cerebrovascular accident in the right parietal lobe, including the semioval center (Figure 1). Given the time elapsed since the onset of symptoms exceeding 4.5 hours, the patient was not a candidate for intravenous thrombolysis, nor did he meet the imaging or clinical criteria for mechanical thrombectomy. The neurology department expanded its investigations to determine the etiology of the stroke in this young patient. A carotid Doppler ultrasound was requested and showed no significant atheromatous plaques, but did reveal findings consistent with vertebrobasilar insufficiency. The transthoracic echocardiogram showed no septal defects, valvular heart disease, patent foramen ovale, or cardiometabolic sources. Blood tests were uneventful, with a lipid profile showing triglycerides 158 mg/dL, LDL cholesterol 52 mg/dL, and HDL cholesterol 15 mg/dL, and a coagulation profile showing prothrombin time (PT) 12 seconds and partial thromboplastin time (PTT) 28 seconds. 
Given the patient's age, the absence of associated risk factors, and the suspicion of a prothrombotic state, markers for autoimmune diseases were requested, with positive results for lupus anticoagulant and IgG anticardiolipin antibodies (Table 1), which led us to suspect primary antiphospholipid syndrome as the cause of the stroke. Viral serology tests are requested for hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). The HIV test is reactive, so viral load and Western Blot tests are requested for confirmation, confirming the presence of infection with a viral load of 1,117,549 and a CD4 count of 23 cells/microl, which tested positive for human immunodeficiency virus type I (Table 1).
Treatment begins with high-intensity statins, antiplatelet agents (acetylsalicylic acid), anticoagulants based on vitamin K antagonists (VKA), prophylaxis for opportunistic infections, as well as antiretroviral therapy and physical rehabilitation to enable the patient to resume basic and instrumental activities of daily living. Confirmation of antiphospholipid antibody positivity was performed at 12 weeks (Table 2). The INR targets are monitored very closely, as they are currently not on target. Currently progressing well and undergoing multidisciplinary follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 34-year-old male presented to the emergency department on June 9, 2025 with sudden-onset left-sided facial, upper, and lower extremity paresthesias, left-sided muscle stiffness, and left hemiparesis upon awakening.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: At approximately 8:30 a.m. on June 9, 2025, upon waking, the patient experienced sudden-onset paresthesias and predominantly distal dysesthesias involving the left face and left upper and lower extremities lasting ~2 hours, accompanied by left-sided muscle stiffness and weakness with preserved consciousness and speech. He presented to the emergency department more than 4.5 hours after symptom onset.
subjective.past_medical_history: No known chronic degenerative diseases; family history negative for autoimmune diseases or thromboembolic events.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for left hemibody paresthesia/dysesthesia, stiffness, and weakness; negative for loss of consciousness or aphasia.

objective.physical_examination: Initial vital signs: blood pressure 126/76 mmHg, heart rate 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, SpO2 94% on room air, and temperature 36.2 °C. Neurological examination showed GCS 15, NIHSS score of 12, left upper and lower limb motor strength of 3/5 (Daniels scale), decreased fine touch sensation in the left upper limb, and a left upper motor neuron syndrome with left lower extremity hyperreflexia, spastic hypertonia, and a positive left Babinski sign.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood tests showed triglycerides 158 mg/dL, LDL cholesterol 52 mg/dL, HDL cholesterol 15 mg/dL, PT 12 seconds, and PTT 28 seconds. Autoimmune prothrombotic workup was positive for lupus anticoagulant and IgG anticardiolipin antibodies (confirmed positive on repeat testing at 12 weeks). Viral serologies were negative for HBV and HCV and reactive for HIV. Carotid Doppler ultrasound showed no significant carotid atheroma but suggested vertebrobasilar insufficiency.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count was 23 cells/µL. Non-contrast head CT demonstrated an acute-to-subacute ischemic stroke in the right parietal lobe involving the centrum semiovale. Transthoracic echocardiogram excluded valvular disease, septal defects, patent foramen ovale, or cardioembolic sources.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Acute right parietal ischemic stroke (NIHSS 12) secondary to antiphospholipid syndrome (persistent lupus anticoagulant and IgG anticardiolipin positivity confirmed at 12 weeks) unmasking previously undiagnosed advanced HIV-1 infection (confirmed by reactive HIV screening, positive HIV-1 Western blot, plasma HIV-1 viral load of 1,117,549 copies/mL, and CD4+ T-cell count of 23 cells/µL). Because presentation exceeded the 4.5-hour window and thrombectomy criteria, acute reperfusion was not performed; he was initiated on high-intensity statin therapy, aspirin, vitamin K antagonist (VKA) oral anticoagulation with close INR monitoring, opportunistic infection prophylaxis, antiretroviral therapy, and physical rehabilitation, with favorable functional recovery on multidisciplinary follow-up.
